where we have used ⟨O^J;p⟩\langle\hat{O}_{J;p}\rangle as shorthand for the matrix element ⟨jN||O^J;p||jN⟩\langle j_{N}||\hat{O}_{J;p}||j_{N}\rangle.

The pattern one sees in the above results reflects an underlying EFT power counting. Suppose we designate our WIMP-nucleon operators as 𝒪i​(αi,βi)\mathcal{O}_{i}(\alpha_{i},\beta_{i}) where αi\alpha_{i} and βi\beta_{i} denote the number of powers of v→⟂\vec{v}^{\perp} and q→/mN\vec{q}/m_{N}, respectively, appearing in the operator,

𝒪i​(αi,βi)↔[v→⟂]αi​[q→mN]βiαi=0,1.\displaystyle\mathcal{O}_{i}(\alpha_{i},\beta_{i})\leftrightarrow\left[\vec{v}^{\perp}\right]^{\alpha_{i}}~\left[{\vec{q}\over m_{N}}\right]^{\beta_{i}}~~~~\alpha_{i}=0,1. (71)

The total cross section has the form

σi​(v)∼ci2​μT2​(v2)αi+βi​(μT2mN2)βi​[aTi​⟨O^iT⟩2+aNi​δαi​1​⟨O^iN⟩2​(μT2mN2)αi]\displaystyle\sigma_{i}(v)\sim c_{i}^{2}~\mu_{T}^{2}~(v^{2})^{\alpha_{i}+\beta_{i}}\left({\mu_{T}^{2}\over m_{N}^{2}}\right)^{\beta_{i}}\left[a_{T}^{i}\langle\hat{O}_{i}^{T}\rangle^{2}+a^{i}_{N}\delta_{\alpha_{i}1}\langle\hat{O}_{i}^{N}\rangle^{2}\left({\mu_{T}^{2}\over m_{N}^{2}}\right)^{\alpha_{i}}~\right] (72)

where O^iT\hat{O}_{i}^{T} and O^IN\hat{O}_{I}^{N} represent one of the dimensionless point (M0,Σ1′,Σ1′′)(M_{0},\Sigma^{\prime}_{1},\Sigma^{\prime\prime}_{1}) or composite (Δ1,Φ~2,Φ0,2′′)(\Delta_{1},\tilde{\Phi}_{2},\Phi^{\prime\prime}_{0,2}) operators, respectively, and aTia_{T}^{i} and aNia_{N}^{i} represent simple numerical factors, e.g.,

aT15=Sχ​(Sχ+1)18aN15=2​Sχ​(Sχ+1)3typically​with​aNiaTi∼10.\displaystyle a_{T}^{15}={S_{\chi}(S_{\chi}+1)\over 18}~~~~~~~~a_{N}^{15}={2S_{\chi}(S_{\chi}+1)\over 3}~~~~~\mathrm{typically~with}~~{a_{N}^{i}\over a_{T}^{i}}\sim 10. (73)

We see that total cross sections and thus total rates depend on the dimensionless parameters vv and μT/mN\mu_{T}/m_{N}, but that the parametric dependence on μT/mN\mu_{T}/m_{N} depends on the operator type, point or composite. The cross section for the composite operators have the simple behavior

σi​(v)|N∼[v2​μT2mN2]αi+βi.\displaystyle\sigma_{i}(v)\Big|_{N}\sim\left[v^{2}{\mu_{T}^{2}\over m_{N}^{2}}\right]^{\alpha_{i}+\beta_{i}}. (74)

where the value of αi+βi\alpha_{i}+\beta_{i}=0,1,2,3 is equivalent to our EFT designation LO, NLO, NNLO, N3LO. This reflects the fact that there are αi+βi\alpha_{i}+\beta_{i} powers of q→/mN\vec{q}/m_{N} in the composite operator, with one factor (αi=1\alpha_{i}=1) coming from i​q→⋅x→​(i)i\vec{q}\cdot\vec{x}(i) in combination with v→N​(i)\vec{v}_{N}(i). The cross section contributions of the point-nucleus operator scale as

σi​(v)|T∼(v2)αi​[v2​μT2mN2]βi.\displaystyle\sigma_{i}(v)\Big|_{T}\sim(v^{2})^{\alpha_{i}}~\left[v^{2}{\mu_{T}^{2}\over m_{N}^{2}}\right]^{\beta_{i}}. (75)

There are βi\beta_{i} powers of q→/mN\vec{q}/m_{N}, while the accompany velocity is not a nuclear operator, but the c-number vT⟂v^{\perp}_{T}.

Both terms are generally present (see the exception below) if there is a velocity coupling. Consequently the neglect of composite operators for interactions with derivative couplings not only leads to a cross section that is much too small (by a factor ∼(aNi/aTi)​(μT2/mN2)\sim(a_{N}^{i}/a_{T}^{i})(\mu_{T}^{2}/m_{N}^{2})), but produces a cross section with the wrong parametric dependence on mTm_{T} and mχm_{\chi}, potentially distorting comparisons among experiments that are using different nuclear targets, as well as sensitivity plots as a function of mχm_{\chi}.

If this calculation is extended to the full operators rather than just there long-wavelength forms, the two terms comprising Eq. (72) are modified by factors FT2​(γ)F^{2}_{T}(\gamma) and FN2​(γ)F_{N}^{2}(\gamma), where γ=(b​μT​v)2\gamma=(b\mu_{T}v)^{2}. Thus three dimensionless parameters, vv, γ\gamma, and μT/mN\mu_{T}/m_{N}, describe the total cross section’s dependence on the WIMP velocity, the nuclear size, and the WIMP-to-nucleus mass ratio, respectively.

4.4 Comparison of the Standard and EFT Results

The above results should be helpful to those wanting to understand the limitations of standard treatments that retain only the Fermi and Gamow-Teller responses. The consequences are operator specific:

  1. 1.

    Operators 𝒪1\mathcal{O}_{1} and 𝒪4\mathcal{O}_{4} are the simple-minded spin-independent and spin-dependent operators. Their coupling is to total spin and total charge (in the general case, some combination of N and Z, depending on chosen operator isospin). These operators are point operators, and thus the standard treatment is valid in all respects.

  2. 2.

    The coupling of operator 𝒪11\mathcal{O}_{11} to the nucleus is 1i1_{i}, the vector charge operator. As the nuclear physics is identical to that of 𝒪1\mathcal{O}_{1}, a standard spin-independent analysis would correctly model the nuclear physics of this operator. However, the dependence of rates on the WIMP velocity distribution differ for 𝒪1\mathcal{O}_{1} and 𝒪11\mathcal{O}_{11}, and this difference would normally not be addressed in comparisons among experiments if only interaction 𝒪1\mathcal{O}_{1} is retained (see point 7 below).

  3. 3.

    The operators 𝒪6\mathcal{O}_{6} and 𝒪10\mathcal{O}_{10} couple to the nucleus through longitudinal spin, q→⋅σ→​(i)\vec{q}\cdot\vec{\sigma}(i), while 𝒪9\mathcal{O}_{9} couples through transverse spin, q→×σ→​(i)\vec{q}\times\vec{\sigma}(i). For these operators, the standard analysis based on a spin-dependent coupling would yield the right threshold (q→→0\vec{q}\rightarrow 0) coupling to the nucleus, but misrepresent the form factors (as Σ′\Sigma^{\prime} and Σ′′\Sigma^{\prime\prime} are described by distinct form factors). The predicted dependence of rates on the galactic WIMP velocity distribution also differs from the standard 𝒪4\mathcal{O}_{4} interaction (see point 7 below).

  4. 4.

    The operators 𝒪3\mathcal{O}_{3}, 𝒪5\mathcal{O}_{5}, 𝒪8\mathcal{O}_{8}, 𝒪12\mathcal{O}_{12}, 𝒪13\mathcal{O}_{13}, and 𝒪15\mathcal{O}_{15} involve velocity-dependent couplings to the nucleus. The standard spin-independent/spin-dependent analysis grossly misrepresents the physics of these operators, leading to errors that can exceed several orders of magnitude. They couple dominantly through the new composite operators Δ\Delta, Φ~′\tilde{\Phi}^{\prime}, and Φ′′\Phi^{\prime\prime}: the contributions of these operators to the cross section are parametrically enhanced relative to those of the standard operators by the factor (4−24)×(μT/mN)2∼10​A2(4-24)\times(\mu_{T}/m_{N})^{2}\sim 10A^{2}. The resulting large errors can be partially mitigated in the case of 𝒪5\mathcal{O}_{5} and 𝒪8\mathcal{O}_{8} because the new operators compete with M0M_{0}, which can be coherent if isospin couplings are dialed to make the operator primarily isoscalar. But even in this favorable case, the error can be an order of magnitude.

  5. 5.

    In all of the cases above, the standard treatment would distort the multipolarity of the coupling. Operators 𝒪3\mathcal{O}_{3}, 𝒪12\mathcal{O}_{12}, 𝒪13\mathcal{O}_{13}, and 𝒪15\mathcal{O}_{15} would appear in the standard treatment as spin-dependent interactions, coupling through Σ1′\Sigma_{1}^{\prime} and Σ1′′\Sigma_{1}^{\prime\prime}, and thus could be probed only if the target has jN≥1/2j_{N}\geq 1/2. In fact, 𝒪3\mathcal{O}_{3}, 𝒪12\mathcal{O}_{12}, and 𝒪15\mathcal{O}_{15} have dominant scalar couplings through Φ0′′\Phi_{0}^{\prime\prime}, which we have noted is proportional to σ→​(i)⋅l→​(i)\vec{\sigma}(i)\cdot\vec{l}(i) – an operator that is not only scalar, but is quasi-coherent, as discussed in [1]. The dominant contribution from 𝒪13\mathcal{O}_{13} is through the tensor operator Φ~2′\tilde{\Phi}^{\prime}_{2}, which requires jN≥1j_{N}\geq 1, a possibility totally outside the standard description.

  6. 6.

    Two operators remain that at first appear puzzling: 𝒪7\mathcal{O}_{7} and 𝒪14\mathcal{O}_{14} have velocity-dependent couplings to the nucleus, but unlike the operators discussing in point 5, they have standard spin-dependent couplings, and no contribution from the new composite operators. This result is a consequence of the good P and CP of nuclear wave functions. These operators couple to the nucleus through the axial-charge, S→N⋅v→⟂\vec{S}_{N}\cdot\vec{v}^{\perp}. When one combines S→N⋅v→⟂\vec{S}_{N}\cdot\vec{v}^{\perp} with e−iq→⋅x→ie^{-i\vec{q}\cdot\vec{x}_{i}} to produce multipole operators in the standard way, the matrix elements of the even multipoles vanish by parity, while those of the odd multipoles vanish by CP (or, equivalently, time-reversal invariance). Consequently all contributions of intrinsic velocities to 𝒪7\mathcal{O}_{7} and 𝒪14\mathcal{O}_{14} vanish. Thus the only contribution to the axial charge operator that survives is the single degree-of-freedom corresponding to the nuclear center-of-mass velocity. As this velocity is a c-number, the associated nuclear coupling is a conventional spin operator, Σ1′\Sigma_{1}^{\prime}.

  7. 7.

    By adopting an interaction having the form 𝒪1\mathcal{O}_{1} or 𝒪4\mathcal{O}_{4}, one builds in the assumption that detector rates depend on the v0v^{0} moment of the galactic velocity distribution. This assumption is generally in error for operators other than 𝒪1\mathcal{O}_{1} and 𝒪4\mathcal{O}_{4}, even if the operator is one of those described in points 2 and 3 above, with nuclear physics quite similar to 𝒪1\mathcal{O}_{1} and 𝒪4\mathcal{O}_{4}. The rates for LO, NLO, NNLO,…, operators depend on the v0v^{0}, v2v^{2}, v4v^{4}, …, moments, respectively, of the WIMP velocity distribution. Consequent the distribution of events as a function of recoil energy ERE_{R} could be used to discriminate among classes of candidate interactions.

5 Nuclear Structure Input: Density Matrices

The Mathematica script described in Sec. 7 is designed to allow a nuclear structure theorist to supply alternative descriptions of the nuclear physics, without requiring him/her to have any detailed knowledge of the operator matrix elements that must be calculated. This is accomplished through the use of density matrices.

The dark matter particle scattering cross sections are expressed in terms of the single-reduced (in angular momentum) matrix elements of one-body operators of definite angular momentum. In the treatment so far we have labeled the nuclear ground state by its angular momentum jNj_{N}, an exact quantum number. Here we add to that label the isospin quantum numbers T,MTT,M_{T}: isospin TT is an approximate but not exact quantum label, as isospin is broken by the electromagnetic interactions among nucleons. However, we employ that label here because most shell-model calculations are isospin conserving, and thus most density matrices derived from such calculations employ TT as a quantum label. We stress, however, that everything discussed below can be trivially repeated without the assumption of TT as a nuclear state label: the density matrix would then be defined without this assumption.

The reduced (in angular momentum) many-body matrix element of an arbitrary one-body operator can be expressed as a product of the one-body density matrix and the single-particle matrix elements of the one-body operator. For our elastic case,

⟨jN;T​MT​‖∑i=1AO^J;τ​(q​x→i)‖​jN;T​MT⟩\displaystyle\langle j_{N};TM_{T}||\sum_{i=1}^{A}\hat{O}_{J;\tau}(q\vec{x}_{i})||j_{N};TM_{T}\rangle =\displaystyle= (−1)T−MT​(TτT−MT0MT)​⟨jN;T​⋮​⋮​∑i=1AO^J;τ​(q​x→i)​⋮​⋮​jN;T⟩\displaystyle(-1)^{T-M_{T}}\left(\begin{array}[]{ccc}T&\tau&T\\ -M_{T}&0&M_{T}\end{array}\right)\langle j_{N};T~\vdots\vdots\sum_{i=1}^{A}\hat{O}_{J;\tau}(q\vec{x}_{i})\vdots\vdots~j_{N};T\rangle
⟨jN;T​⋮​⋮​∑i=1AO^J;τ​(q​x→i)​⋮​⋮​jN;T⟩\displaystyle\langle j_{N};T~\vdots\vdots\sum_{i=1}^{A}\hat{O}_{J;\tau}(q\vec{x}_{i})\vdots\vdots~j_{N};T\rangle =\displaystyle= ∑|α|,|β|Ψ|α|,|β|J;τ​⟨|α|​⋮​⋮​OJ;τ​(q​x→)​⋮​⋮​|β|⟩.\displaystyle\sum_{|\alpha|,|\beta|}\Psi_{|\alpha|,|\beta|}^{J;\tau}~\langle|\alpha|~\vdots\vdots O_{J;\tau}(q\vec{x})\vdots\vdots~|\beta|\rangle. (79)

Here Ψ|α|,|β|J;τ\Psi_{|\alpha|,|\beta|}^{J;\tau} is the one-body density matrix for the diagonal ground-state-to-ground-state transition; |α||\alpha| represents the nonmagnetic quantum numbers in the chosen single-particle basis (e.g., for a single-particle harmonic oscillator state |α⟩=|nα(lαsα=1/2)jαmjα;tα=1/2mtα⟩≡||α|;mjαmtα⟩|\alpha\rangle=|n_{\alpha}(l_{\alpha}s_{\alpha}=1/2)j_{\alpha}m_{j_{\alpha}};t_{\alpha}=1/2m_{t_{\alpha}}\rangle\equiv||\alpha|;m_{j_{\alpha}}m_{t_{\alpha}}\rangle, with nαn_{\alpha} the nodal quantum number); ⋮​⋮\vdots\vdots denotes a doubly reduced matrix element (in spin and isospin); and the sums over |α||\alpha| and |β||\beta| extend over complete sets of single-particle quantum numbers. The density matrix can be written in second quantization as

Ψ|α|,|β|J;τ≡1(2​J+1)​(2​τ+1)​⟨jN;T​⋮​⋮​[c|α|†⊗c~|β|]J;τ​⋮​⋮​jN;T⟩\displaystyle\Psi_{|\alpha|,|\beta|}^{J;\tau}\equiv{1\over\sqrt{(2J+1)(2\tau+1)}}~\langle j_{N};T~\vdots\vdots\left[c_{|\alpha|}^{\dagger}\otimes\tilde{c}_{|\beta|}\right]_{J;\tau}\vdots\vdots~j_{N};T\rangle (80)

where the single particle creation operator is cα†c^{\dagger}_{\alpha} while c~β=(−1)jβ−mjβ+1/2−mtβ​c|β|;−mjβ,−mtβ\tilde{c}_{\beta}=(-1)^{j_{\beta}-m_{j_{\beta}}+1/2-m_{t_{\beta}}}c_{|\beta|;-m_{j_{\beta}},-m_{t_{\beta}}}. The phases yield a destruction operator c~β\tilde{c}_{\beta} that transforms as a spherical tensor in single-particle angular momentum and isospin.

Equation (79) is an exact expression for ⟨jN;TMT||O^J;τ||jN;TMT⟩\langle j_{N};TM_{T}||\hat{O}_{J};\tau||j_{N};TM_{T}\rangle. When one invokes a nuclear model to calculate a dark-matter response function, effectively one is employing some physics-motivated prescription for intelligently truncating the infinite sums over |α|,|β||\alpha|,|\beta| in Eq. (79) to some finite subset, hopefully capturing most of the relevant low-momentum physics.

This expression factors a matrix element into a product of density matrix elements, which are independent of any details of the operator O^J;τ\hat{O}_{J;\tau} apart from its rank in angular momentum and isospin, and single-particle operator matrix elements. The Mathematica script calculates the latter, assuming that the single-particle basis for the Slater determinants is the harmonic oscillator. Thus one can modify the script to use different nuclear physics input simply by supplying alternative one-body density matrices for the nuclear targets of interest. There is no need to evaluate any operator matrix elements. In making such substitutions (or better, in adding alternative density matrices, so that one can begin to assess nuclear structure uncertainties), users should employ the single-particle conventions of [8], for consistency with those employed in evaluating the single-particle matrix elements of dark-matter operators.

The isospin matrix element in Eq. (79) is easily performed, yielding

⟨|α|​⋮​⋮​O^J;τ⁡(q​x→)​⋮​⋮​|β|⟩=2​(2​τ+1)​⟨nα​(lα​1/2)​jα||OJ||nβ​(lβ​1/2)​jβ⟩\displaystyle\langle|\alpha|~\vdots\vdots\hat{O}_{J};\tau(q\vec{x})\vdots\vdots~|\beta|\rangle=\sqrt{2(2\tau+1)}~~\langle n_{\alpha}(l_{\alpha}1/2)j_{\alpha}~||O_{J}||~n_{\beta}(l_{\beta}1/2)j_{\beta}\rangle (81)

where OJO_{J} is the space-spin part of the operator. For the harmonic oscillator basis used in the Mathematica script, the single-particle reduced matrix element for OJ={MJO_{J}=\{M_{J}, ΣJ′\Sigma^{\prime}_{J}, ΣJ′′\Sigma^{\prime\prime}_{J}, ΔJ\Delta_{J}, Φ~J′\tilde{\Phi}^{\prime}_{J}, ΦJ′′}\Phi^{\prime\prime}_{J}\} can be evaluated algebraically,

⟨nα​(lα​1/2)​jα||OJ​(q​x→)||nβ​(lβ​1/2)​jβ⟩=14​π​y(J−K)/2​e−y​p​(y)\displaystyle\langle n_{\alpha}(l_{\alpha}1/2)j_{\alpha}||O_{J}(q\vec{x})||n_{\beta}(l_{\beta}1/2)j_{\beta}\rangle={1\over\sqrt{4\pi}}y^{(J-K)/2}e^{-y}p(y) (82)

where K=2K=2 for the normal parity (π=(−1)J\pi=(-1)^{J}) operators MJM_{J}, Φ~J′\tilde{\Phi}_{J}^{\prime}, and Φ~J′′\tilde{\Phi}_{J}^{\prime\prime} and K=1K=1 for the abnormal parity (π=(−1)J+1\pi=(-1)^{J+1}) operators Δ\Delta, Σ′\Sigma^{\prime}, and Σ′′\Sigma^{\prime\prime}. y=(q​b/2)2y=(qb/2)^{2} where bb is the oscillator parameter, and p⁡(y)p(y) is a finite polynomial in yy. Thus the nuclear response functions WW of Eq. (53) are simple functions of yy.

6 Particle Theory Input: Nonrelativistic Matching

In most cases a theorist interested in a given ultraviolet theory of dark matter will derive a relativistic WIMP-nucleon interaction ℒint\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{int}}. The Mathematica script is set up to allow one to 1) input the coefficients cic_{i} of the nonrelativistic Galilean-invariant operators 𝒪i\mathcal{O}_{i} directly (the choice one would likely make in experimental analysis); or alternatively 2) input the coefficients djd_{j} of a set of such covariant interactions amplitudes ℒintj\mathcal{L}^{j}_{\mathrm{int}}, which are then reduced to the form ∑ici​𝒪i\sum_{i}c_{i}\mathcal{O}_{i}.

6.1 The ℒi​n​tj\mathcal{L}^{j}_{int}

In Sec. 2 we discussed two simple examples of 2), the spin-independent and spin-dependent interactions ℒintSI\mathcal{L}^{\mathrm{SI}}_{\mathrm{int}} and ℒintSD\mathcal{L}^{\mathrm{SD}}_{\mathrm{int}}. The invariant amplitudes obtained from these ℒ\mathcal{L} were reduced to their nonrelativistic forms, yielding matrix elements between Pauli spinors. The nonrelativistic operators between the Pauli spinors were identified as 𝒪1\mathcal{O}_{1} and 𝒪4\mathcal{O}_{4}. Here we repeat the process for large set of ℒi​n​tj\mathcal{L}_{int}^{j} listed in Table 1. Unlike the simple cases discussed in Sec. 2, the ℒi​n​tj\mathcal{L}_{int}^{j} do not always map onto single nonrelativistic operators 𝒪j\mathcal{O}_{j}. Instead the result is frequently

ℒintj→∑ici​(j)​𝒪i.\displaystyle\mathcal{L}^{j}_{\mathrm{int}}~\rightarrow~\sum_{i}c_{i}(j)\mathcal{O}_{i}. (83)

where several ci​(j)c_{i}(j) are nonzero.

The interactions of Table 1, coded into our Mathematic script, describe the interactions of spin-1/2 WIMPS with nucleons. (More general interactions could be considered, of course.) Four-momentum definitions follow our three-momentum conventions: the incoming (outgoing) four-momentum of the dark matter particle χ\chi is pμp^{\mu} (p′μp^{\prime\,\mu}); the incoming (outgoing) four-momentum of the nucleon NN is kμk^{\mu} (k′μk^{\prime\,\mu}); and the momentum transfer qμ=p′μ−pμ=kμ−k′μq^{\mu}=p^{\prime\,\mu}-p^{\mu}=k^{\mu}-k^{\prime\,\mu}. We also define Pμ=pμ+p′μP^{\mu}=p^{\mu}+p^{\prime\,\mu} and Kμ=kμ+k′μK^{\mu}=k^{\mu}+k^{\prime\,\mu}. The relative velocity operator of Eq. (14) can be written in term of these variables as

v→⟂≡12​(v→χ,in+v→χ,out−v→N,in−v→N,out)=12​(P→mχ−K→mN).\displaystyle\vec{v}^{\perp}\equiv{1\over 2}\left(\vec{v}_{\chi,\mathrm{in}}+\vec{v}_{\chi,\mathrm{out}}-\vec{v}_{N,\mathrm{in}}-\vec{v}_{N,\mathrm{out}}\right)={1\over 2}\left({\vec{P}\over m_{\chi}}-{\vec{K}\over m_{N}}\right). (84)

The relativistic WIMP-nucleon interactions are constructed as bilinear WIMP-nucleon products of the available scalar (χ¯​χ\bar{\chi}\chi, χ¯​γ5​χ\bar{\chi}\gamma^{5}\chi) and four-vector (χ¯​Pμ​χ\bar{\chi}P^{\mu}\chi, χ¯​Pμ​γ5​χ\bar{\chi}P^{\mu}\gamma^{5}\chi, χ¯​i​σμ​ν​qν​χ\bar{\chi}i\sigma^{\mu\nu}q_{\nu}\chi, and χ¯​γμ​γ5​χ\bar{\chi}\gamma^{\mu}\gamma^{5}\chi) amplitudes. Thus there are 22+42=202^{2}+4^{2}=20 combinations [1]. The nonrelativistic operators obtained after nonrelativistic reduction are listed in Table 1, along with the corresponding expansions in terms of our EFT operators, the 𝒪i\mathcal{O}_{i}. The Table also gives transformation properties of the interactions under parity and time-reversal. Note that all interactions reduce in leading order to combinations of our fifteen 𝒪i\mathcal{O}_{i}, and all of the 𝒪i\mathcal{O}_{i} appear in the Table. Thus they are the minimal set of nonrelativistic interactions needed to represent the listed set of 20 ℒi​n​tj.\mathcal{L}^{j}_{int}.

6.2 Units: Inputing the djd_{j}s into the Mathematic Script

The Mathematica script allows one to specific an interaction corresponding to an arbitrary sum over the terms in Table 1. It then calculates the corresponding operator, expressing it in terms of the 𝒪i\mathcal{O}_{i}, that one uses between Paul spinors to calculate the WIMP-nucleon (Galilean) invariant amplitude. Thus

∑jdj​ℒi​n​tj→∑ici​𝒪i\displaystyle\sum_{j}d_{j}\mathcal{L}_{int}^{j}\rightarrow\sum_{i}c_{i}\mathcal{O}_{i} (85)

where the cic_{i} are functions of the {dj}\{d_{j}\}. The ℒi​n​tj\mathcal{L}_{int}^{j} of the Table all have the same dimension, as the dimensionless quantities Pμ/mMP_{\mu}/m_{M}, Kμ/mMK_{\mu}/m_{M} and qμ/mMq_{\mu}/m_{M} were used in the operator construction. Here mMm_{M} is a mass scale that will generally be known, given a model context. The djd_{j}, like the cjc_{j}, have dimensions 1/mass2. Hence the conversion of a djd_{j} to a linear combination of the cic_{i} involves an expression with only dimensionless coefficients.

In analogy with input for the cjc_{j}, the djd_{j} are input in units of 1/mM21/m_{M}^{2}. That is

input​dj=1⇒dj=1/mM2.\displaystyle\mathrm{input~}d_{j}=1\Rightarrow d_{j}=1/m_{M}^{2}. (86)

The user is queried about the desired input value for mMm_{M}. If no value is specified, the script defaults to the choice mM=mv=246.2m_{M}=m_{v}=246.2 GeV, weak interaction strength. Note that the value of mMm_{M} is used both in Eq. (86), converting input numbers into appropriately dimensioned couplings djd_{j}, as well as in defining the momentum-dependent operators appearing in the Table.

7 The Mathematica Script: Documentation

The formalism presented in this paper, with its factorization cross sections into products of WIMP and nuclear responses, is the basis for the Mathematica script presented here. The script was constructed so that experimental groups would be able to conduct model independent analyses of their experiments using the EFT framework. We have integrated the particle and nuclear physics in ways that should make the code useful to nuclear structure and particle theorists as well, as described in previous sections.

In this section, which also serves as a readme file for the program, we discuss the usage of the program itself.

7.1 Initialization

Our Mathematica package, along with all of the associated documentation, can be found at
http://www.ocf.berkeley.edu/~nanand/software/dmformfactor/. To initialize the package, either put dmformfactor.m in your directory for Mathematica packages and run

<<‘dmformfactor

or initialize the package file itself from its source directory. For example

<<"/Users/me/myfiles/dmformfactor.m"

7.2 Summary of Functions

In order to compute the WIMP response functions Riτ​τ′​(v→T⟂2,q→ 2mN2)R_{i}^{\tau\tau^{\prime}}(\vec{v}_{T}^{\perp 2},{\vec{q}^{\,2}\over m_{N}^{2}}), the user must first call functions setting the dark matter mass and spin as well as the coefficients of the effective Lagrangian. In order to compute the nuclear response functions Wi​((q​b/2)2)W_{i}((qb/2)^{2}), the user must specify the ZZ and AA of the isotope. The density matrices and the oscillator parameter bb needed in the calculation of the WiW_{i} are set internally in the script, though there are options to override the internal values. The nuclear ground state spin and isospin (the script assumes exact isospin, consistent with an input density matrix that is doubly reduced - see text) are also set internally, once ZZ and AA are input.

  • •

    SetJChi and SetMChi: These set the dark matter spin and mass, respectively. Simply call:

    SetJChi[j]

    and

    SetMChi[m]

    to set the dark matter spin to j and the dark matter mass to m. The unit GeV is recognized by the script; for example, calling SetMChi[10 GeV] sets the dark matter mass to 10 GeV.

  • •

    SetIsotope[Z,A,bFM, filename]

    This sets the nuclear physics input, including the charge Z and atomic number A of the isotope, the file for the density matrices that the user wants to use, and the oscillator parameter b⁡[fm]b[\textrm{fm}] (that is, bb in femtometers). If the users elects to use the default density matrices (which are available for 19F, 23Na, 70Ge, 72Ge, 73Ge, 74Ge, 76Ge, 127I, 128Xe, 129Xe, 130Xe, 131Xe, 132Xe, 134Xe, and 136Xe), then simple take filename to be “default” (note that one must still specify the correct Z and A for the isotope of interest. Otherwise, users must provide their own density matrix file, to be read in by the program. Similarly, entering “default” for bb will employ the approximate formula b⁡[fm]=41.467/(45A−1/3−25A−2/3)b[\textrm{fm}]=\sqrt{41.467/(45A^{-1/3}-25A^{-2/3})}. To use another value of b⁡[fm]b[\textrm{fm}], enter a numerical value. The nuclear mass is set to A​mNAm_{N}.

  • •

    SetCoeffsNonrel[i,value,isospin]

    This sets the coefficients cic_{i} of the EFT operators 𝒪i\mathcal{O}_{i}. The script allows the user to set values for {c1,c3,c4,…,c15}\{c_{1},c_{3},c_{4},...,c_{15}\}; note that c2c_{2} is excluded, for reasons discussed in the text. We have chosen a normalization such that the coefficients cic_{i} all have dimensions (Energy)−2(\textrm{Energy})^{-2};11 1 Note that this convention for the cic_{i}’s differs from that in [1]. to compensate for this, the dimensionless user input for value is multiplied by mV−2m_{V}^{-2}, with mV≡246.2m_{V}\equiv 246.2 GeV.

    The coefficients carry an isospin index α\alpha that can be specified in one of two ways, as a coupling to protons and neutrons, {cip,cin}\{c_{i}^{p},c_{i}^{n}\}, in which case the associated operator is

    [cip​1+τ32+cin​1−τ32]​𝒪i\displaystyle\left[c_{i}^{p}{1+\tau_{3}\over 2}+c_{i}^{n}{1-\tau_{3}\over 2}\right]\mathcal{O}_{i} (87)

    or as a coupling to isospin, {ci0,ci1}\{c_{i}^{0},c_{i}^{1}\}, where the associated operator is

    [ci0+ci1​τ3]​𝒪i.\displaystyle\left[c_{i}^{0}+c_{i}^{1}\tau_{3}\right]\mathcal{O}_{i}. (88)

    For the former, the input should be “n” for neutrons and “p” for protons. For example:

    SetCoeffsNonrel[4,12.3, "p"]

    whereas for the latter it should be 0 for isoscalar and 1 for isovector. All coefficients are set to 0 by default when the package is initialized. SetCoeffsNonrel will change only the coefficient specified, and will leave all other coefficients unchanged. So, for example, if one initializes the package and calls SetCoeffsNonrel[4,12.3, 0], then c4pc_{4}^{p} and c4nc_{4}^{n} will both be 6.15, with all other coefficients vanishing. If one then calls SetCoeffsNonrel[4,3.3,``p''], then c4pc_{4}^{p} will be set to 3.3, but c4nc_{4}^{n} will not change and will still be 6.15. Thus by making two calls, an arbitrary combination of {c4p,c4n}\{c_{4}^{p},c_{4}^{n}\} or equivalently {c40,c41}\{c_{4}^{0},c_{4}^{1}\} can be set.

  • •

    SetCoeffsRel[i,value,isospin]

    These functions are similar to SetCoeffsNonrel, except that they set the coefficients djd_{j} of the 20 covariant interactions ℒintj\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{int}}^{j} defined in Table 1. The coefficients djd_{j} are dimensionless, by inserting appropriate powers of the user-defined scale mMm_{M}, set by the user function SetMM. This scale is set by default to be mM=mV≡246.2m_{M}=m_{V}\equiv 246.2 GeV. We adopt a convention where the spinors in ℒintj\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{int}}^{j} are defined as normalized to unity: with this convention a nonrelativistic reduction of the ℒintj\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{int}}^{j} in the second column of Table 1 would give the results in the fourth column. [As noted in the paper, we use a spinor normalization of 2​m2m in our derivations, but extract the factor of 4​mχ​mN4m_{\chi}m_{N} in order to maintain the definition above.]

    SetCoeffsNonrel and SetCoeffsRel cannot be used together. By default, the package assumes you will use SetCoeffsNonrel. The first time the user calls SetCoeffsRel, the package will first reset all coefficients back to zero before calling SetCoeffsRel, after which point it will act normally. A subsequent call to SetCoeffsNonrel will similarly first reset all coefficients back to zero and then revert to non-relativistic mode.

    Since the relativistic operators implicitly assume spin-1/2 WIMPs, any call to SetCoeffsRel automatically sets jχ=1/2j_{\chi}=1/2.

  • •

    SetMM[mM]

    Set the fiducial scale mMm_{M} for the relativistic coefficients did_{i}.

  • •

    ZeroCoeffs[]

    Calling ZeroCoeffs[] simply resets all operators coefficients to zero.

  • •

    ResponseNuclear[y,i,tau,tau2]

    This function prints out any of the eight nuclear response functions Wiτ​τ2​(y)W_{i}^{\tau\tau_{2}}(y). This involves a folding of the single-particle matrix elements with the density matrices. The results are printed as analytic functions in the dimensionless variable y=(q​b/2)2y=(qb/2)^{2}. The ii run from 1 to 8, according to 1) WMW_{M}, 2) WΣ′′W_{\Sigma^{\prime\prime}}, 3) WΣ′W_{\Sigma^{\prime}}, 4) WΦ′′W_{\Phi^{\prime\prime}}, 5) WΦ~′W_{\tilde{\Phi}^{\prime}}, 6) WΔW_{\Delta}, 7) WM​Φ′′W_{M\Phi^{\prime\prime}}, and 8) WΣ′​ΔW_{\Sigma^{\prime}\Delta}.

  • •

    TransitionProbability[v,q(,IfRel)]

    This is the main user function. It first prints out the Lagrangian that is being used.

    Second, it folds the Wiτ​τ′​(y)W_{i}^{\tau\tau^{\prime}}(y) and Riτ​τ′​(v→T⟂2,q→ 2mN2)R_{i}^{\tau\tau^{\prime}}(\vec{v}_{T}^{\perp 2},{\vec{q}^{\,2}\over m_{N}^{2}}) to form

    Ptot=12​jχ+1​12​jN+1​∑spins|ℳ|nucleus−HO/EFT2,\displaystyle P_{\rm tot}={1\over 2j_{\chi}+1}{1\over 2j_{N}+1}\sum_{\mathrm{spins}}|\mathcal{M}|^{2}_{\mathrm{nucleus-HO/EFT}}, (89)

    It then evaluates the transition probability for the numerical values of bb and mNm_{N}. As bb is in fm, the substitution is y=(q​b/(2​ℏ​c))2∼(q​b/2​(0.197​Gev​fm))2y=(qb/(2\hbar c))^{2}\sim(qb/2(0.197\mathrm{Gev~fm}))^{2}. As mNm_{N} is input in GeV, this evaluates Eq. (52) as a function TransitionProbability[vsq,q] where q is in GeV. This function can be printed out or plotted numerically.

    The conventional relativistic normalization of the amplitude differs from the non-relativistic normalization by a factor of 1/(4​mχ​mT)1/(4m_{\chi}m_{T}). Since the conventional relativistic normalization is commonly used and produces a dimensionless value for |ℳ|2|\mathcal{M}|^{2}, we also provide an optional argument IfRel, which if set to True will output (89) with the relativistic normalization convention (that is, it will multiply by (4​mχ​mT)2(4m_{\chi}m_{T})^{2} to produce a dimensionless transition probability). By default, it is set to False.

  • •

    DiffCrossSection[ERkeV,v]

    From the transition probability PtotP_{\rm tot}, one can immediately obtain the differential cross section per recoil energy:

    d​σd​ER\displaystyle\frac{d\sigma}{dE_{R}} =\displaystyle= mT2​π​v2​Ptot.\displaystyle\frac{m_{T}}{2\pi v^{2}}P_{\rm tot}. (90)

    The function DiffCrossSection[ERkeV,v] takes as arguments the recoil energy in units of keV and the velocity of the incoming DM particle in the lab frame. It first prints out the Lagrangian being used, and then outputs the differential cross-section d​σd​ER\frac{d\sigma}{dE_{R}}.

  • •

    ApproxTotalCrossSection[v]

    From the differential cross-section d​σd​ER\frac{d\sigma}{dE_{R}}, one can also obtain the total cross-section as a function of vv by integrating over recoil energies. In general, this depends on energy thresholds and, written in closed form, is a complicated analytic function due to the exponential damping factor e−2​ye^{-2y} in the response functions, so for precise values it is simplest to do the energy integration numerically. However, for approximate results we can consider the limit of small nuclear harmonic oscillator parameter bb, in which case the exponential factor e−2​ye^{-2y} can be neglected. For fixed vv, the integration over ERE_{R} from zero up to the kinematic threshold ER,max=2​μT2​v2mTE_{R,\rm max}=2\frac{\mu_{T}^{2}v^{2}}{m_{T}} can be performed analytically. The function ApproxTotalCrossSection[v] takes as argument the velocity vv of the incoming DM particle in the lab frame and, after printing out the Lagrangian being used, outputs this approximate total cross-section σ⁡(v)\sigma(v).

  • •

    EventRate[NTN_{T},ρχ\rho_{\chi},qq,vev_{e},v0v_{0}(,vescv_{\rm esc})]

    One can determine the total detector event rate (per unit time per unit detector mass per unit recoil energy) in terms of the transition probability PtotP_{\rm tot}. One simply multiplies PtotP_{\rm tot} by the appropriate prefactor and integrates over the halo velocity distribution, as follows:

    d​RDd​ER=NT​ρχ​mT2​π​mχ​⟨1v​Ptot​(v2,q2)⟩\displaystyle\frac{dR_{D}}{dE_{R}}=N_{T}\frac{\rho_{\chi}m_{T}}{2\pi m_{\chi}}\left\langle\frac{1}{v}P_{\rm tot}(v^{2},q^{2})\right\rangle (91)

    Here, ⟨…⟩\langle\dots\rangle indicates averaging over the halo velocity distribution. NTN_{T} is the number of target nuclei per detector mass, ρχ\rho_{\chi} is the local dark matter density, mχm_{\chi} is the dark matter mass, and mNm_{N} is the nucleon mass. In general, the halo average integral should include a lower-bound on the magnitude of the velocity at vminv_{\rm min}, which is vmin=q2​μTv_{\rm min}=\frac{q}{2\mu_{T}} for elastic scattering:

    ⟨h⁡(q,v→)⟩\displaystyle\langle h(q,\vec{v})\rangle ≡\displaystyle\equiv ∫vmin​(q)∞v2​𝑑v​∫d2​Ω​fv​(v→+v→e)​h​(q,v→).\displaystyle\int_{v_{\rm min}(q)}^{\infty}v^{2}dv\int d^{2}\Omega f_{v}(\vec{v}+\vec{v}_{e})h(q,\vec{v}). (92)

    The vector v→e\vec{v}_{e} is the Earth’s velocity in the galactic rest frame. While there has been much work recently on understanding theoretical constraints on the halo distribution from N-body simulations and from general considerations of dynamics, little is known by direct observation and there are still large uncertainties. A very simple approximation that suffices for general considerations is to take a Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution:

    fv​(v→)\displaystyle f_{v}(\vec{v}) =\displaystyle= 1π3/2​v03e−v2/v02,\displaystyle\frac{1}{\pi^{3/2}v_{0}^{3}}e^{-v^{2}/v_{0}^{2}}, (93)

    where v0v_{0} is roughly 220 km/s, about the rms velocity of the visible matter distribution (though N-body simulations suggest that the dark matter distribution may be shallower, and a larger v0v_{0} may be more appropriate). The function EventRate[q,b,ve,v0] evaluates the event rate d​RDd​ER\frac{dR_{D}}{dE_{R}} assuming this Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution as default. A cut-off Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution is also implemented as an option, in which case

    fv​(v→)\displaystyle f_{v}(\vec{v}) ∝\displaystyle\propto (e−v2/v02−evesc2/v02)Θ(vesc2−v→2)\displaystyle\left(e^{-v^{2}/v_{0}^{2}}-e^{v_{\rm esc}^{2}/v_{0}^{2}}\right)\Theta(v_{\rm esc}^{2}-\vec{v}^{2}) (94)

    where vescv_{\rm esc} is the escape velocity, and the subtraction above is included to make the distribution shut down smoothly. In this case, vescv_{\rm esc} should be included as an optional argument to EventRate; if it is not included, it is set to a default value of 12​v012v_{0} (which is essentially vesc=∞v_{\rm esc}=\infty).

  • •

    SetHALO[halo]

    This sets the halo distribution used. The variable h​a​l​ohalo can be set either to “MB”, in which case the Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution is used, or “MBcutoff”, in which case the cut-off Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution is used. It is set to “MB” by default.

  • •

    SetHelm[UseHelm]

    Calling SetHelm[True] sets the structure function for the density operator MJM_{J} to be given by the Helm form factor, rather than by the structure function obtained from the density matrix. SetHelm[False] implements the structure function based on the density matrix, which is the default setting.

7.3 Examples

A full example for the transition probability would look like the following:

<< "/Users/me/mypackages/dmformfactor.m";SetJChi[1/2]SetMChi[50 GeV]F19filename="default";bFM="default";SetIsotope[9, 19, bFM, F19filename]SetCoeffsNonrel[3, 3.1, "p"]TransitionProbability[v,qGeV]TransitionProbability[v,qGeV,True]

To additionally calculate the event rate d​RDd​ER\frac{dR_{D}}{dE_{R}} in a Maxwell-Boltzmann halo velocity distribution, one can call

mNucleon=0.938 GeV;NT=1/(19 mNucleon);Centimeter=(10^13 Femtometer);rhoDM=0.3 GeV/Centimeter^3;ve=232 KilometerPerSecond;v0=220 KilometerPerSecond;EventRate[NT,rhoDM,qGeV,ve,v0]

For a cut-off Maxwell-Boltzmann halo, an escape velocity must also be specified:

mNucleon=0.938 GeV;NT=1/(19 mNucleon);Centimeter=(10^13 Femtometer);rhoDM=0.3 GeV/Centimeter^3;ve=232 KilometerPerSecond;v0=220 KilometerPerSecond;vesc=550 KilometerPerSecond;SetHalo["MBcutoff"];EventRate[NT,rhoDM,qGeV,ve,v0,vesc]

Finally, to get a quick estimate of the experimental bound from the 225 live day run of XENON100, one can use the standard spin-independent isoscalar interaction for a generic isotope of xenon, taking xenon-131 for instance. Taking into account efficiencies, the total effective exposure is approximately 2500 kg days. A relativistic operator coefficient of 2​fp/GeV22f_{p}/{\rm GeV}^{2} with fp=4⋅10−9f_{p}=4\cdot 10^{-9} predicts only a couple of events, and so should be close to the upper limit of their allowed cross-section:

mNucleon=0.938 GeV;NT=1/(131 mNucleon);Centimeter=(10^13 Femtometer);rhoDM=0.3 GeV/Centimeter^3;SetMChi[150 GeV]ve=232 KilometerPerSecond;v0=220 KilometerPerSecond;vesc=550 KilometerPerSecond;SetHALO["MBcutoff"];Xe131filename="default";bFM="default";SetIsotope[54, 131, bFM, Xe131filename]SetCoeffsRel[1,2fp,0]myrate[qGeV_]=(2500 KilogramDay) EventRate[NT,rhoDM,qGeV,ve,v0,vesc];fp=2.4*10^(-4);NIntegrate[myrate[qGeV] GeV*(qGeV GeV/(131 mNucleon)),{qGeV,0,10}]

The final line of output should be 2.06 for the value of the integral, which gives the predicted number of events. The factor q131​mN=qmT\frac{q}{131m_{N}}=\frac{q}{m_{T}} inside the integral is from the change of variables from d​ERdE_{R} to d​qdq, since ER=q2/2​mTE_{R}=q^{2}/2m_{T}. In this example, the WIMP is sufficiently heavy that the exact low-energy threshold changes the prediction by less than a factor of two, so to get a rough estimate we have just integrated down to zero energy. Finally, we can look what nucleon scattering cross-section corresponds to fp=2.4⋅10−4f_{p}=2.4\cdot 10^{-4}:

σp\displaystyle\sigma_{p} =\displaystyle= (4​mN​mT​fp/mV2)216​π​(mN+mT)2=1.7⋅10−45​cm2\displaystyle\frac{(4m_{N}m_{T}f_{p}/m_{V}^{2})^{2}}{16\pi(m_{N}+m_{T})^{2}}=1.7\cdot 10^{-45}{\rm cm}^{2} (95)

which agrees to within a factor of a few with the published upper bound on σp\sigma_{p} from the XENON100 collaboration [9]. A more accurate calculation of the bound would include, among other corrections, the exact energy thresholds in the integral over momentum transfer, an average over the year as the earth’s velocity changes, a sum over different isotopes according to their natural abundance, and a more precise treatment of energy-dependent efficiencies.

7.4 Density Matrix Syntax

If one calls SetIsotope[Z,A, filename] with a custom density matrix, the input density matrix file must contain the reduced density matrix elements ΨJ,T​(|α|,|β|)\Psi^{J,T}(|\alpha|,|\beta|) to be used. The in and out states |α||\alpha| and |β||\beta| should be specified by their principle quantum number NN and their total angular momentum jj. See [10] for more details. The format of the file for each projection onto operators of spin JJ and isospin JJ should be as follows:

ONE-BODY DENSITY MATRIX       ⋯\cdots       2J0= 2​J2J,  ⋯\cdots  2​T2T

⋯\cdots Nin1N^{1}_{\rm in}   2​jin12j^{1}_{\rm in}   Nout1N^{1}_{\rm out}   2​jout12j^{1}_{\rm out}   ΨJ,T​({Nin1,jin1},{Nout1,jout1})\Psi^{J,T}\left(\{N^{1}_{\rm in},j^{1}_{\rm in}\};\{N^{1}_{\rm out},j^{1}_{\rm out}\}\right)

⋮        ⋮        ⋮

⋯\cdots NinnN^{n}_{\rm in}   2​jinn2j^{n}_{\rm in}   NoutnN^{n}_{\rm out}   2​joutn2j^{n}_{\rm out}   ΨJ,T​({Ninn,jinn},{Noutn,joutn})\Psi^{J,T}\left(\{N^{n}_{\rm in},j^{n}_{\rm in}\};\{N^{n}_{\rm out},j^{n}_{\rm out}\}\right)

Dots “⋯\cdots” indicate places where the code will simply ignore what appears there - the routines reading in the input are searching for regular expressions that match the above syntax. Consequently, additional lines in the file that are not of the above form will also be ignored. This is probably clearest to follow by seeing an explicit example. For instance, the density matrix for 19F is:

Appendix A Appendix: Some Details of the Response Function Derivation

The algebraic techniques that lead to Eq. (49) are commonly used in treatments of semi-leptonic weak interactions. We will briefly outline the steps, after first taking note of certain simplifications that are made in the many-body theory to obtain the relatively tractable form of Eq. (49).

A.1 Treatment of the velocity operator

We take as our WIMP-nucleus interaction the sum over the one-body interactions of the WIMP with the individual nucleons in the nucleus. While this is the usual starting point for treatments of electroweak nuclear reactions, it is an assumption. The nucleon is a composite object held together by the exchange of various mesons, which clearly can have their own interactions with the WIMP. There has been some work on the possible size of two-body corrections to WIMP-nucleus interactions [11, 12]. Our feeling at this point is that the uncertainty of the WIMP interaction with nucleons, as embodied in our fourteen coefficients cic_{i}, is currently so great that the one-body approximation is appropriate. This sentiment would change were dark matter interactions discovered, making a detailed understanding WIMP-matter interactions important.

Given the assumption of a one-body interaction, we noted that the Galilean invariance then leads to the replacement

v→⟂\displaystyle\vec{v}^{\perp} →\displaystyle\rightarrow {12(v→χ,in+v→χ,out−v→N,in(i)−v→N,out(i)),i=1,….,A}\displaystyle\left\{{1\over 2}\left(\vec{v}_{\chi,\mathrm{in}}+\vec{v}_{\chi,\mathrm{out}}-\vec{v}_{N,\mathrm{in}}(i)-\vec{v}_{N,\mathrm{out}}(i)\right),i=1,....,A\right\} (96)
≡\displaystyle\equiv v→T⟂−{v˙→N,in​(i)+v˙→N,out​(i),i=1,…,A−1}.\displaystyle\vec{v}_{T}^{\perp}-\left\{\vec{\dot{v}}_{N,\mathrm{in}}(i)+\vec{\dot{v}}_{N,\mathrm{out}}(i),i=1,...,A-1\right\}.

The DM particle/nuclear center of mass relative velocity is a c-number,

v→T⟂=12​(v→χ,in+v→χ,out−v→T,in​(i)−v→T,out​(i))\displaystyle\vec{v}_{T}^{\perp}={1\over 2}\left(\vec{v}_{\chi,\mathrm{in}}+\vec{v}_{\chi,\mathrm{out}}-\vec{v}_{T,\mathrm{in}}(i)-\vec{v}_{T,\mathrm{out}}(i)\right)

while the A−1A-1 internal nuclear Jacobi velocities v˙→N\vec{\dot{v}}_{N} are operators acting on intrinsic nuclear coordinates. It may be helpful to illustrate this division more explicitly, using one of our interactions, the axial charge operator 𝒪7\mathcal{O}_{7}. We take the simplest example of two nucleons in a nucleus. Then

v→⟂⋅S→N\displaystyle\vec{v}^{\perp}\cdot\vec{S}_{N} →\displaystyle\rightarrow ∑i=1212​(v→χ,in+v→χ,out−v→N,in​(i)−v→N,out​(i))⋅S→N​(i)\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{2}\frac{1}{2}\left(\vec{v}_{\chi,\rm in}+\vec{v}_{\chi,\rm out}-\vec{v}_{N,\rm in}(i)-\vec{v}_{N,\rm out}(i)\right)\cdot\vec{S}_{N}(i) (97)
=\displaystyle= 12​(v→χ,in+v→χ,out−v→N,in​(1)+v→N,in​(2)2−v→N,out​(1)+v→N,out​(2)2)⋅∑i=12S→N​(i)\displaystyle\frac{1}{2}\left(\vec{v}_{\chi,\rm in}+\vec{v}_{\chi,\rm out}-{\vec{v}_{\rm N,in}(1)+\vec{v}_{\rm N,in}(2)\over 2}-{\vec{v}_{N,\rm out}(1)+\vec{v}_{N,\rm out}(2)\over 2}\right)\cdot\sum_{i=1}^{2}\vec{S}_{N}(i)

yields one term proportional to v→T⟂\vec{v}_{T}^{\perp},

v→T⟂≡12​(v→χ,in+v→χ,out−v→T,in−v→T,out)wherev→T≡12​∑i=12v→​(i)\displaystyle\vec{v}_{T}^{\perp}\equiv\frac{1}{2}\left(\vec{v}_{\chi,\rm in}+\vec{v}_{\chi,\rm out}-\vec{v}_{T,\rm in}-\vec{v}_{T,\rm out}\right)~~~~\mathrm{where}~~~~\vec{v}_{T}\equiv{1\over 2}\sum_{i=1}^{2}\vec{v}(i) (98)

and a second term that depends only on the relative inter-nucleon velocity, and is thus separately Galilean invariant. This decomposition can be repeated for A nucleons

∑i=1A12​(v→χ,in+v→χ,out−v→N,in​(i)−v→N,out​(i))⋅S→N​(i)=v→T⟂⋅∑i=1AS→N​(i)−[∑i=1A12​(v→N,in​(i)+v→N,out​(i))⋅S→N​(i)]i​n​t\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{A}\frac{1}{2}\left(\vec{v}_{\chi,\rm in}+\vec{v}_{\chi,\rm out}-\vec{v}_{N,\rm in}(i)-\vec{v}_{N,\rm out}(i)\right)\cdot\vec{S}_{N}(i)=\vec{v}_{T}^{\perp}\cdot\sum_{i=1}^{A}\vec{S}_{N}(i)-\left[\sum_{i=1}^{A}\frac{1}{2}\left(\vec{v}_{N,\rm in}(i)+\vec{v}_{N,\rm out}(i)\right)\cdot\vec{S}_{N}(i)\right]_{int}

where v→T\vec{v}_{T} is now the target velocity obtained by averaging over AA nucleon velocities. The intrinsic operator on the right can be written in a form that makes the dependence on relative nucleon velocities manifest

12​A​∑i>j=1A(S→N​(i)−S→N​(j))⋅[(v→N,in​(i)+v→N,out​(i))−(v→N,in​(j)+v→N,out​(j))]\displaystyle{1\over 2A}\sum_{i>j=1}^{A}\left(\vec{S}_{N}(i)-\vec{S}_{N}(j)\right)\cdot\left[\left(\vec{v}_{N,\rm in}(i)+\vec{v}_{N,\rm out}(i)\right)-\left(\vec{v}_{N,\rm in}(j)+\vec{v}_{N,\rm out}(j)\right)\right] (99)

or, alternatively and trivially, it can be written as the difference of two terms

∑i=1A12​(v→N,in​(i)+v→N,out​(i))⋅S→N​(i)−12​[v→T,in+v→T,out]⋅∑i=1AS→N​(i).\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{A}\frac{1}{2}\left(\vec{v}_{N,\rm in}(i)+\vec{v}_{N,\rm out}(i)\right)\cdot\vec{S}_{N}(i)-{1\over 2}\left[\vec{v}_{T,\mathrm{in}}+\vec{v}_{T,\mathrm{out}}\right]\cdot\sum_{i=1}^{A}\vec{S}_{N}(i). (100)

The above discussion was presented to clarify how the velocity operator is separated into its v→T⟂\vec{v}_{T}^{\perp} and intrinsic nuclear pieces, but also to illustrate two assumptions made in our development,

  • •

    The assumption that the WIMP-nuclear interaction is the sum over the individual WIMP-nucleon interactions leads to two interactions that are separately Galilean invariant, one constructed from v→T⟂\vec{v}_{T}^{\perp} and one constructed from the internal relative nucleon velocities. However these two interactions then have a common coefficient, c7c_{7}. In contrast, if one were to construct an effective theory at the nuclear level, operators that are separately invariant would be assigned independent strengths. It would be interesting to explore whether the work of [11, 12] on more complicated WIMP-nucleus couplings can be viewed as adding corrections to the one-body formulation that, in fact, make the two operators independent.

  • •

    While the nuclear matrix elements in the formulas we derive in the text are intrinsic ones, in fact almost all calculations of the structure of complex nuclei are performed in overcomplete bases in which the coordinates of all AA nucleons appear. If the underlying single-particle basis is the harmonic oscillator and if set of included Slater determinants is appropriately chosen, certain separability properties of the harmonic oscillator allow one to remove the extra degrees of freedom by numerical means, forcing the center-of-mass into the 1​s1s state. Yet still the basis is expressed in terms of nucleon coordinates. Largely for this reason, the intrinsic operator is evaluated using Eq. (100) with the f​u​r​t​h​e​rfurther assumption that the second, more complicated term in Eq. (100) can be ignored. This clearly greatly simplifies the calculation, allowing one to evaluate the nuclear matrix element from the one-body density matrix. This kind of approximation – or more correctly, simplification – is used almost universally in nuclear physics, as there is no practical alternative. In schematic models it can be shown that the errors induced are typically o⁡(1/A)o(1/A) and associated with a center-of-mass form factor.

⟨l⟩≡⟨jχ​Mχ​f|l|jχ​Mχ​i⟩\langle l\rangle\equiv\langle j_{\chi}M_{\chi f}|l|j_{\chi}M_{\chi i}\rangle (108)

Note that while our original multipole decomposition was done with a z-axis aligned along q→\vec{q}, this result is now frame independent as it is expressed entirely in terms of scalar products

Finally, we average over initial WIMP spins and sum over final spins, as in the nuclear case. The WIMP tensors involve combinations of 1 and S→χ\vec{S}_{\chi}. As we sum over all magnetic quantum numbers, the only surviving terms in the bilinear products of the WIMP tensors must transform as spin scalars, and thus as 1 or as S→χ 2\vec{S}_{\chi}^{\,2}. The constant term yields 1. All cross terms linear in S→χ\vec{S}_{\chi} must vanish. The spin terms must be proportional to jχ​(jχ+1)j_{\chi}(j_{\chi}+1). The associated coefficients are easily calculated for the various products

12​jχ+1​∑mχi​mχf⟨jχ​mχi|{S→χ​|jχ​mχf⟩⋅⟨jχ​mχf|​S→χA→⋅S→χ​|jχ​mχf⟩​⟨jχ​mχf|​B→⋅S→χA→×S→χ​|jχ​mχf⟩⋅⟨jχ​mχf|​B→×S→χA→×S→χ​|jχ​mχf⟩⋅⟨jχ​mχf|​S→χ}|jχ​mχi⟩={1A→⋅B→/32​A→⋅B→/30}​jχ​(jχ+1)\displaystyle{1\over 2j_{\chi}+1}\sum_{m_{\chi_{i}}m_{\chi_{f}}}\langle j_{\chi}m_{\chi_{i}}|\left\{\begin{array}[]{c}\vec{S}_{\chi}|j_{\chi}m_{\chi_{f}}\rangle\cdot\langle j_{\chi}m_{\chi_{f}}|\vec{S}_{\chi}\\[4.26773pt] \vec{A}\cdot\vec{S}_{\chi}|j_{\chi}m_{\chi_{f}}\rangle~~\langle j_{\chi}m_{\chi_{f}}|\vec{B}\cdot\vec{S}_{\chi}\\[4.26773pt] \vec{A}\times\vec{S}_{\chi}|j_{\chi}m_{\chi_{f}}\rangle\cdot\langle j_{\chi}m_{\chi_{f}}|\vec{B}\times\vec{S}_{\chi}\\[4.26773pt] \vec{A}\times\vec{S}_{\chi}|j_{\chi}m_{\chi_{f}}\rangle\cdot\langle j_{\chi}m_{\chi_{f}}|\vec{S}_{\chi}\end{array}\right\}|j_{\chi}m_{\chi_{i}}\rangle=\left\{\begin{array}[]{c}1\\[5.40608pt] \vec{A}\cdot\vec{B}/3\\[5.40608pt] 2\vec{A}\cdot\vec{B}/3\\ 0\end{array}\right\}j_{\chi}(j_{\chi}+1)

The results are further simplified because the resulting scalars A→⋅B→\vec{A}\cdot\vec{B} often involve longitudinal and transverse quantities or q→⋅v→T⟂\vec{q}\cdot\vec{v}_{T}^{\perp}, which vanish.

Executing the associated algebra yields the final result given in Eqs. (49) and (50). The transition probability is expressed as a product of WIMP and nuclear responses functions, where the former isolates the particle physics in functions that are bilinear in the EFT coefficients, the cic_{i}s.

A.3 Generalizing the Exchange

Our EFT approach has focused on interactions between the WIMP and nucleus mediated by a heavy exchange, so that the interaction is pointlike. However, nothing in the treatment of the WIMP or nuclear vertices depends on this assumption. We believe the adaptation of this code for cases in which the exchange is mediated by a photon or other light particle would be very simple. This would, of course, require one to add the needed momentum-dependent propagator to the code. Once that line is added, however, we see no reason that subsequent integrations over phase space would present any difficulties: indeed the operator formalism we employ here is the common formalism for both electron scattering and semi-leptonic weak interactions. The exchange in the former is a photon, while the latter is treated as a four-fermion interaction analogous to the WIMP case.
